title: Two suspects in Mountie slaying were on parole
article: As grief-stricken relatives, friends and colleagues prepare to say goodbye to slain Manitoba RCMP Constable Dennis Strongquill this week, the revelation that two men suspected of killing him were out on parole has sparked an investigation by the government agencies that oversee Canada's parole system.

Robert Marlo Sand, 23, of Westlock, Alta., and Laurie Anne Bell, 20, of Edmonton, will appear in a Brandon, Man., court this week on a charge of first-degree murder. They were captured Friday afternoon in a shootout with RCMP outside a motel in Wolseley, Sask., in which police shot and killed 21-year-old Danny Wayne Sand, Robert Sand's brother.

The Correctional Service of Canada and the National Parole Board have launched a joint investigation into the supervision of the Sand brothers, who had both recently been released from federal prison and were wanted for parole violation. A preliminary review should be completed today.

The dramatic capture Friday ended a 14-hour manhunt. Constable Strongquill, a 52-year-old father of six and a 20-year veteran of the RCMP, was gunned down early Friday morning in Russell, Man., near the Manitoba-Saskatchewan boundary. The incident began when he and partner Brian Auger pulled over a pickup truck for failing to dim its high-beam headlights.

The killers fired on the officers, then chased them as they retreated to town, ramming the police cruiser and fatally shooting Constable Strongquill when the officers stopped their vehicle outside the Russell RCMP headquarters.

Constable Strongquill's friends and co-workers spent the weekend trying to come to grips with the death of the likable Mountie, who was the senior officer in a recently formed all-aboriginal detachment at the Waywayseecappo reserve near Russell.
"It's like losing a family member. You are just kind of numb," said Sergeant Sonny Richards, head of the five-person detachment where Constable Strongquill had transferred just a few months ago.

Constable Strongquill became a father for the sixth time last month, when Amanda Delaronde of Barrows, Man., gave birth to a baby girl, their first child together. The officer had five children from a previous relationship.
"He just loved his job. He told me he could never, ever think of doing anything else," Sgt. Richards said. "First and foremost, his greatest passion was his children."

A memorial service will be held Thursday afternoon in Powerview, Man., where Constable Strongquill was stationed for several years and where members of his family still live. Police officers from across North America are expected to attend. There will be a private wake Friday and a private funeral Saturday in Barrows, about 200 kilometres north of Russell.

Robert Sand walked away from an Edmonton halfway house two weeks ago, after being released on day parole Nov. 1, three years into a seven-year sentence for robbery. Danny Sand got out of prison Sept. 28 after serving the mandatory two-thirds of a two-year term for possession of property obtained by crime, possession of a weapon and dangerous driving. A warrant was issued for his arrest Friday when he failed to show up for a meeting with his parole officer in Edmonton.

"Whenever there is an incident regarding a federal offender in the community, the normal course of action would be for us to undertake a review and investigation," said Tim Krause, spokesman for the correctional service.
He said that in particularly serious cases, the correctional service and the parole board conduct a joint investigation.
